questions.prompt: Given `constexpr int a(int x) { return x + 1; }` and `consteval int b(int x) { return x + 1; }`, what happens when `main` calls both with a non-constant local `int n = 5;`?
options: Both `a(n)` and `b(n)` compile and run at runtime.
`a(n)` compiles and runs at runtime, while `b(n)` is a compile error.
`a(n)` is a compile error because `n` is not constant, while `b(n)` compiles.
Both `a(n)` and `b(n)` fail to compile because `n` is not `constexpr`.
questions.explanation: A `constexpr` function may execute either at compile time or at runtime depending on the call context, so `a(n)` runs cleanly at runtime. A `consteval` function is an immediate function (`[dcl.consteval]`) whose every evaluation must be a compile-time constant expression, so `b(n)` is ill-formed.

questions.prompt: When should you declare a namespace-scope variable `constinit` instead of `constexpr`?
options: When the variable is a local automatic variable inside a function.
When the initializer depends on runtime user input.
When you want the variable to have internal linkage automatically.
When you want guaranteed static initialization to avoid initialization-order bugs while still mutating the variable at runtime.
questions.explanation: `constinit` (`[dcl.constinit]`) requires constant initialization for a variable with static or thread storage duration—preventing dynamic initialization order bugs—without making the variable `const`. `constexpr` makes the variable implicitly `const`.

questions.prompt: What is the bug in `compute(int x)` below when invoked with a runtime integer `n`?
options: `std::is_constant_evaluated()` cannot be called in an `if constexpr` condition.
It returns `x + 1` at runtime and `x * 2` at compile time.
The `if constexpr` condition is manifestly constant-evaluated, so `std::is_constant_evaluated()` is always `true` and the `else` branch is discarded.
The code fails to compile because `x` is not a template parameter.
questions.explanation: The condition of `if constexpr` is always evaluated as a constant expression (`[stmt.if]`), so `std::is_constant_evaluated()` unconditionally returns `true` there. Even when `compute(n)` is called at runtime, it executes `x * 2`. Use plain `if (std::is_constant_evaluated())` in C++20 or `if consteval` in C++23.

questions.prompt: Which declaration using `std::vector` compiles cleanly in C++23?
options: `constexpr std::size_t n = vec_len();` compiles, while `constexpr auto v = make_vec();` fails.
Both `constexpr std::size_t n = vec_len();` and `constexpr auto v = make_vec();` compile.
Neither compiles because `std::vector` allocates dynamic heap memory.
`constexpr auto v = make_vec();` compiles only if `v` is declared `constinit`.
questions.explanation: C++20/23 supports transient allocation (`[expr.const]/5`): compile-time `new` and `delete` are permitted inside `vec_len()` because `v` is destroyed and freed before evaluation completes. Returning `std::vector` into a `constexpr` variable attempts to retain unfreed allocation past constant evaluation, which is ill-formed.

questions.prompt: Why does calling a `consteval` helper `ce(x)` compile inside `if consteval` in C++23 when it fails inside `if (std::is_constant_evaluated())`?
options: `if consteval` converts the parameter `x` into a template parameter automatically.
The compound statement of `if consteval` is an immediate-function context, whereas an ordinary `if` block is not.
`std::is_constant_evaluated()` is deprecated in C++23 and forbidden with `consteval`.
Inside `if consteval`, `ce(x)` is silently rewritten into a runtime call.
questions.explanation: Under `[stmt.if]` and `[expr.const]`, the true branch of `if consteval` places expressions in an immediate-function context, allowing calls to `consteval` functions using non-constant parameters of the enclosing `constexpr` function. A plain `if (std::is_constant_evaluated())` does not create an immediate context.

questions.prompt: What does the C++ standard require when evaluating a `constexpr` variable initializer triggers signed integer overflow (`INT_MAX + 1`)?
options: It wraps around cleanly using two's complement arithmetic.
It compiles with a warning and stores an unspecified value.
It only fails if `-Werror` or `-fsanitize=undefined` is enabled.
The program is ill-formed because any undefined behavior disqualifies a core constant expression.
questions.explanation: `[expr.const]/5` explicitly disqualifies any evaluation that triggers undefined behavior in the abstract machine from being a core constant expression. Since `constexpr` requires a constant expression initializer, the compiler must emit a diagnostic.
